--- title: "ASM Chapter 4" author: "Alun ap Rhisiart" date: "10/12/2026" categories: [code, julia, statistics, asm, ecology] execute: echo: true warning: false output: true engine: julia --- We turn to Chapter 4 of Applied Statistical Modelling for Ecologists, by Marc Kéry and Kenneth Kellner. IN this chapter we turn to a comparison of different statistical modelling approaches for ecological data. The book considers jagsUI, NIMBLE, TMB, Stan, and Maximum Likelihood. I add Turing.jl to the mix, with a brief discussion of other Julia packages. First we pull in any packages we will need. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using DataFramesMeta, Distributions, StatsBase, StatsPlots, RCall, MCMCChains, MCMCDiagnosticTools ``` ::: First, let's make sure we have the exact same random variables as the book, for direct comparison. To ensure this, we actually call the R code itself, rather than use any of Julia's RNGs. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} R""" set.seed(4) y10 <- rnorm(n = 10, mean = 600, sd = 30) # Sample of 10 birds y1000 <- rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 600, sd = 30) """ @rget y10 y1000 truth = (mean=600, sd=30) first(y1000, 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 10-element Vector{Float64}: 616.9981349454094 600.4715836201372 611.4917201555145 598.6458865226008 601.0305572219098 605.0708032265492 634.9508051708302 598.6738800824373 596.9889467224228 591.4966629337923 ``` ::: ::: Next, eyeball the data, which will check that it looks the same as in the book. ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} p1 = histogram(y10, color=:grey, xlims=(500, 700), bins=5, xlabel="y10", ylabel="Frequency", legend=false ) p2 = histogram(y1000, color=:grey, bins=10, xlabel="y1000", legend=false ) # 3. Combine in a 1x2 layout plot(p1, p2, layout=(1, 2), size=(800, 400)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: For the 'canned' example, the book uses lm(). We can use GLM.jl for this. It takes an object that implements the Tables.jl inteface, not a vector, so we just wrap it in a DataFrame. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using GLM y10lm = lm(@formula(y10 ~ 1), DataFrame(y10=y10)) y1000lm = lm(@formula(y1000 ~ 1), DataFrame(y1000=y1000)) y1000lm ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` StatsModels.TableRegressionModel{LinearModel{GLM.LmResp{Vector{Float64}}, GLM.DensePredChol{Float64, LinearAlgebra.CholeskyPivoted{Float64, Matrix{Float64}, Vector{Int64}}}}, Matrix{Float64}} y1000 ~ 1 Coefficients: ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Coef. Std. Error t Pr(>|t|) Lower 95% Upper 95% ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── (Intercept) 598.846 0.917595 652.63 <1e-99 597.045 600.647 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ``` ::: ::: ## Maximum Likelihood Estimation To keep in line with the book we will also do this manually, using idiomatic Julia where appropriate. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Random, Optim, ForwardDiff, ADTypes # Optim requires arrays of floats, not integers starts = [550.0, 25.0] # Objective Function (Negative Log-Likelihood) function NLL(param, y) pop_mean = param[1] pop_sd = param[2] # Catch negative standard deviations so the optimizer doesn't crash if pop_sd <= 0.0 return Inf end # Equivalent to -sum(dnorm(y, mean=pop_mean, sd=pop_sd, log=TRUE)) return -loglikelihood(Normal(pop_mean, pop_sd), y) end # Optimize # We use an anonymous function `p -> NLL(p, y1000)` to pass the data # autodiff = AutoForwardDiff() calculates the gradients automatically for faster convergence fm = optimize(p -> NLL(p, y1000), starts, LBFGS(), autodiff = AutoForwardDiff()) # Extract the maximum likelihood estimates mle_estimates = Optim.minimizer(fm) println("MLE Estimates (Mean, SD): ", mle_estimates) # Calculate the Hessian at the minimum (equivalent to R's hessian=TRUE) H = ForwardDiff.hessian(p -> NLL(p, y1000), mle_estimates) println("Hessian Matrix:\n", H) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` MLE Estimates (Mean, SD): [598.8460950752325, 29.002390678087444] Hessian Matrix: [1.188864620730756 6.827315404646025e-10; 6.827315179674075e-10 2.377729241796953] ``` ::: ::: The book now checks convergence, inverts the 'Hessian', and gets the standard errors for the parameter estimates. We can do the same in Julia as follows: ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using LinearAlgebra # Check convergence converged = Optim.converged(fm) println("Converged: ", converged) # Invert the Hessian to get the covariance matrix cov_matrix = inv(H) println("Covariance Matrix:\n", cov_matrix) # Standard errors for the parameter estimates std_errors = sqrt.(diag(cov_matrix)) println("Standard Errors (Mean, SD): ", std_errors) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Converged: true Covariance Matrix: [0.8411386650444126 -2.415211481758575e-10; -2.415211402173144e-10 0.420569332462874] Standard Errors (Mean, SD): [0.9171361213279153, 0.6485131706163523] ``` ::: ::: ## The Turing.jl model This is the main point about using Julia for Bayesian statistics. Let's build the same model in Turing.jl. Note that as this is running in a Quarto document although I have set chains=4 as I normally would it just runs one chain. Also, with the latest version of Turing, the default chain type has changed, so we explicitly set it to `Chains` in the sampling call to maintain compatibility with the MCMCDiagnosticsTools function below, which are not yet updated to `FlexiChains.VNChain` format. ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Turing @model function model_4_4(mass) # 1. Priors # Note: BUGS dnorm(0, 0.0001) uses precision τ = 0.0001, # which corresponds to variance 10,000 or SD = 100 in Turing. pop_mean ~ Uniform(0, 5000) pop_sd ~ Uniform(1, 100) # Add derived quantity for variance if required pop_var = pop_sd^2 # 3. Likelihood (Vectorized) mass .~ Normal(pop_mean, pop_sd) end # Sampling model = model_4_4(y1000) chains = sample(model, NUTS(), 10000; chains=4, chain_type=Chains) ``` ::: Keep in mind that this is a HMC/NUTS model, so equivalent to the Stan example. To me, at least, the model code is *far* more readable, and the steps needed to compile and run the model also short, simple, and easy to understand. More so than NIMBLE: no configure/build/compile/compile/run sequence, just define the model and sample. And the model itself has no declaring of types, no defined sections for params and data, and the code is Julia, so it has the full range of Julia functions available. Also, there is no likelihood loop, because it can do broadcasting as normal, so it is even shorter than the JAGS model code. One thing to note is that, as it is Julia code, the order matters, unlike JAGS. You have to define variables before you can refer to them. Now we can examine the posterior distribution of the parameters. ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} describe(chains) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: We can also consider pop_var if we wish with the following code (which I do not consider further). ```{{julia}} pop_var_samples = chains[:pop_sd] .^ 2 ``` ## Trace plots Getting trace and density plots from the chains is very straightforward. ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plot(chains; size=(800,600)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: There are lots of other plotting options, shown here: [https://turinglang.org/MCMCChains.jl/stable/statsplots/ Describe shows the main diagnostics, but if we wish we can get more detailed diagnostics using the MCMCDiagnosticTools package, for example: ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} summarystats(chains) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
Summary Statistics

      Symbol    Float64   Float64   Float64     Float64     Float64   Float64  ⋯

    pop_mean   598.8453    0.9167    0.0107   7404.5551   6619.1236    1.0000  ⋯
      pop_sd    29.0391    0.6572    0.0095   4750.5265   4718.5462    0.9999  ⋯

                                                                1 column omitted
``` ::: ::: ::: Or any of the following (and more): - `bfmi(chains)` # updated from gelmandiag - `ess(chains)` # effective sample size for each parameter - `rhat(chains)` # potential scale reduction factor for each parameter - `mcse(chains)` # Monte Carlo standard error for each parameter ### Logical tests For jagsUI (section 4.4.2) the book shows how to do straightforward logical tests, such as `mean(sims[,"pop.mean"] < 597)`. We can do a similar thing with Turing. #### The direct vector extraction way ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # Extract flattened vector of all posterior draws (e.g. 10,000 x 4 = 40,000 draws) pop_mean_draws = vec(Array(chains[:pop_mean])) # Calculate posterior probability P(pop_mean < 597) prob = mean(pop_mean_draws .< 597) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.0231 ``` ::: ::: #### As a one-liner ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # Direct one-liner prob = mean(chains[:pop_mean] .< 597) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.0231 ``` ::: ::: ## Other options besides Turing The Julia ecosystem is a lot less mature than R. Turing itself is mature and stable, but other packages for Bayesian modeling may not be as fully developed or as user-friendly as their R counterparts. ### TuringGLM I tried JuliaBUGS and TuringGLM as well, and could get neither to work. TuringGLM has just been archived, end of August 2026, in favour of newer packages. It would be the equivalent of brms. It is being replaced by TuringRegressions.jl and/or BayesianRegressionModels.jl, which I have not yet tried. There is also Soss.jl which seems to be a Julia interface to the Python library, so will not be considered here. I will try the other two packages and if successful, I will report my findings here. ### JuliaBUGS If TuringGLM is the equivalent of brms, then JuliaBUGS is the equivalent of rjags or jagsui, providing an interface to the JAGS modelling language from within Julia. It does not call the R programs, but runs on top of Turing.jl. This sounds great for someone coming from R. Even better, it refers to a subpackage in R which would allow R users to run their model in Julia. However, the documentation is messy and I could not get either this simple model to work nor the examples in the documentation. Therefore, I will not be considering JuliaBUGS further in this series. ### Gibbs Sampler It is a shame that there is no direct equivalent to a Gibbs sampler in Julia, as they do make handling of discrete variables such as N-Mixture or occupancy models much easier. There is a Gibbs sampler, but it seems to be for combining different samplers within a single framework. However, there is an argument to be made that marginalisation is the best approach. I note that Turing does support Particle Gibbs, but I don't think that is quite the same use case. They provide AbstractMCMC as a common interface for MCMC samplers, which allows for flexibility in choosing different sampling algorithms, and it would seem not too difficult to have a Gibbs sampler for common ecological use cases to be built using it. There is, after all, a Metropolis-Hastings sampler. I'll look into that possibility.
